+## Change data capture (CDC)
+
+Postgres CDC syncs inserts, updates, and deletes from your tables in near real-time. It relies on Postgres's native logical replication, which means your database must be configured correctly before you enable CDC on a table.
+
+### Prerequisites
+
+- **`wal_level` set to `logical`** – Postgres must be configured to write enough information to the write-ahead log (WAL) for logical decoding. This requires a server restart to change.
+- **A replication slot** – PostHog creates and uses a logical replication slot to stream changes. Each CDC source uses one slot, and Postgres retains WAL segments until the slot consumes them.
+- **A publication** – PostHog creates a publication that lists the tables being captured. Tables must be added to the publication to be captured.
+- **Replication permissions** – The database user needs the `REPLICATION` role (or superuser) and `SELECT` on the captured tables.
+- **`max_replication_slots` and `max_wal_senders`** – Must be high enough to accommodate the slots and connections PostHog uses alongside any other consumers.
+
+### Table modes
+
+CDC can be enabled per table, and each table can use a different mode:
+
+- **CDC** – Captures inserts, updates, and deletes. Requires a primary key so changes can be applied to the correct rows.
+- **Incremental** – Syncs new and updated rows using a replication key. Deletes are not captured.
+- **Append only** – Appends new rows using a cursor. Updates and deletes are not captured.
+- **Full table** – Reloads the whole table on every sync.
+
+You can switch a table between modes, but switching to or from CDC may trigger a resync.
+
+### WAL lag and failure conditions
+
+Because Postgres retains WAL until the replication slot consumes it, an inactive or slow CDC sync can cause WAL to accumulate on your database and fill up disk. Watch for:
+
+- **Growing WAL / disk usage** – If a slot is inactive (for example, the source is paused or failing), Postgres keeps WAL segments. Monitor `pg_replication_slots` for `active` and `restart_lsn`, and drop unused slots.
+- **Slot invalidation** – If WAL required by a slot is removed (for example, after `max_slot_wal_keep_size` is exceeded), the slot is invalidated and CDC can no longer resume from where it left off. A full resync is required.
+- **Replica identity** – Tables without a primary key or with `REPLICA IDENTITY` set to `NOTHING` can't emit the data needed to apply updates and deletes.
+- **Schema changes** – Adding or dropping columns on a captured table may require a resync.
+
+If CDC stops capturing, check the source's status in the [sources tab](https://app.posthog.com/data-management/sources) and verify the slot and publication still exist in your database.
+

+## Enabling and disabling CDC after setup
+
+You don't have to decide on CDC when you create the source. The **Configuration** tab of an existing Postgres source has a CDC section where you can turn CDC on or off and tune lag thresholds without deleting and recreating the source (which would lose your schedule and schema history).
+
+### Enabling CDC
+
+1. Go to the [sources tab](https://app.posthog.com/data-management/sources) and open your Postgres source.
+2. Open the **Configuration** tab and find the CDC section.
+3. Choose a management mode: **PostHog-managed** or **self-managed** (see [Slot and publication management](#slot-and-publication-management)). For self-managed, enter the name of the publication you created.
+4. Click **Check CDC compatibility** to re-run the prerequisite checks against your database.
+5. Confirm to enable CDC. PostHog provisions the replication slot (and, in PostHog-managed mode, the publication) and stores the CDC settings on the source.
+
+Enabling CDC doesn't automatically switch existing tables to CDC sync. After enabling, configure individual tables to use the CDC sync method.
+
+### Changing CDC settings
+
+While CDC is enabled, you can edit the WAL lag warning and critical thresholds and the automatic slot protection setting from the same section. The warning threshold must be lower than the critical threshold. Other CDC settings, such as the management mode and slot or publication names, can't be changed after CDC is enabled.
+
+### Disabling CDC
+
+When you disable CDC, PostHog:
+
+- Cancels any running CDC syncs for the source.
+- Removes the CDC extraction schedule.
+- Drops the replication slot, and in PostHog-managed mode the publication too. In self-managed mode, your publication is left untouched.
+- Soft-deletes the `_cdc` history tables.
+- Resets CDC tables so they no longer sync. You'll need to choose a new sync method for each of them.
+
+You can re-enable CDC later. Re-enabling starts from a fresh replication slot, so CDC tables need a new initial snapshot.
+

+### Hive Metastore compatibility
+
+When a table is registered in a Hive Metastore (HMS), the HMS table definition stores the column names and types
+separately from the Iceberg metadata. Some schema-evolution operations can therefore leave the HMS definition out of
+sync with the Iceberg schema, which can cause failures or incorrect results when the table is read through Hive or
+another engine that relies on the HMS definition.
+
+Operations that can be affected include:
+
+* **Rename** -- renaming a column or nested field changes the name in the Iceberg schema, but the HMS definition may
+  still reference the old name.
+* **Drop** -- dropping a column removes it from the Iceberg schema, but the HMS definition may still list it.
+* **Reorder** -- changing the order of columns may not be reflected in the HMS definition.
+
+To avoid these issues, keep the HMS definition in sync with the Iceberg schema. When using Hive, perform schema
+changes through Hive commands so that both definitions are updated together (see [Hive](hive.md#schema-evolution)).
+When schema changes are made by another engine, verify that the HMS definition reflects the new schema before reading
+the table through Hive. If the definitions diverge, the table may need to be re-registered or the HMS definition
+updated to match the Iceberg schema.

+---
+title: Transforming data with add_map
+description: Transforming data before loading using the add_map capability
+keywords: [transforming, add_map, map, customising, pipelines]
+---
+
+# Transforming data with `add_map`
+
+`add_map` lets you apply a function to each item (row) of a resource before it is loaded. It is a flexible way to transform, enrich, or clean your data as it flows through the pipeline. The function you pass receives a single item and must return the transformed item.
+
+## Basic usage
+
+In the example below, we create a dummy source and use `add_map` to add a computed column to each row.
+
+```py
+import dlt
+
+@dlt.source
+def dummy_source():
+    @dlt.resource(write_disposition="replace")
+    def dummy_data():
+        for i in range(3):
+            yield {"id": i, "name": f"Jane Washington {i}"}
+
+    return dummy_data()
+
+def add_greeting(doc):
+    doc["greeting"] = f"Hello, {doc['name']}!"
+    return doc
+
+# 1. Create an instance of the source so you can edit it.
+source_instance = dummy_source()
+
+# 2. Modify this source instance's resource
+source_instance.dummy_data.add_map(add_greeting)
+
+# 3. Inspect your result
+for row in source_instance:
+    print(row)
+# {'id': 0, 'name': 'Jane Washington 0', 'greeting': 'Hello, Jane Washington 0!'}
+# ...
+```
+
+## Applying `add_map` to a resource directly
+
+You can also call `add_map` directly on a resource, which is useful when you want to transform data without creating a source instance first:
+
+```py
+for row in dummy_source().dummy_data.add_map(add_greeting):
+    print(row)
+```
+
+## Using a lambda
+
+For simple transformations, you can pass a lambda function:
+
+```py
+source_instance.dummy_data.add_map(lambda doc: {**doc, "id": doc["id"] * 10})
+```
+
+## Chaining multiple maps
+
+`add_map` returns the resource, so you can chain multiple transformations together. They are applied in the order they are added:
+
+```py
+source_instance.dummy_data.add_map(add_greeting).add_map(
+    lambda doc: {**doc, "name": doc["name"].upper()}
+)
+```
+
+## Running the pipeline
+
+Once you have modified the resource, run the pipeline as usual:
+
+```py
+pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
+    pipeline_name="example",
+    destination="bigquery",
+    dataset_name="transformed_data",
+)
+load_info = pipeline.run(source_instance)
+print(load_info)
+```
+
+:::tip
+`add_map` is applied to each item individually. If you need to filter items, use `add_filter`; if you need to transform the whole batch at once, use `add_yield_map`.
+:::
+

+* [Removing columns.](./removing_columns)

+## AWS S3 Tables and Glue catalogs
+
+When writing Iceberg tables to AWS, you can use one of three catalog setups. All of them require the `pyiceberg` extra and the additional Iceberg permissions described above.
+
+### S3 Tables REST catalog
+
+Uses the S3 Tables REST catalog endpoint. Tables are stored in an S3 Table bucket.
+
+- **Bucket**: an S3 Table bucket (not a regular S3 bucket)
+- **Warehouse**: the table bucket ARN, `arn:aws:s3tables:<region>:<account-id>:bucket/<bucket>`
+- **Endpoint**: `https://s3tables.<region>.amazonaws.com/iceberg`
+- **SigV4 service**: `s3tables`
+
+```toml
+[destination.iceberg]
+catalog_type = "rest"
+
+[destination.iceberg.credentials]
+uri = "https://s3tables.<region>.amazonaws.com/iceberg"
+warehouse = "arn:aws:s3tables:<region>:<account-id>:bucket/<bucket>"
+
+[destination.iceberg.credentials.properties]
+rest.sigv4-enabled = "true"
+rest.signing-region = "<region>"
+rest.signing-name = "s3tables"
+```
+
+### Glue REST catalog with S3 Tables
+
+Uses the AWS Glue REST catalog endpoint backed by an S3 Table bucket. Prepare IAM, Glue, and Lake Formation for S3 Tables before loading.
+
+- **Bucket**: an S3 Table bucket
+- **Warehouse**: the warehouse identifier `<account-id>:s3tablescatalog/<bucket>`
+- **Endpoint**: `https://glue.<region>.amazonaws.com/iceberg`
+- **SigV4 service**: `glue`
+
+```toml
+[destination.iceberg]
+catalog_type = "rest"
+
+[destination.iceberg.credentials]
+uri = "https://glue.<region>.amazonaws.com/iceberg"
+warehouse = "<account-id>:s3tablescatalog/<bucket>"
+
+[destination.iceberg.credentials.properties]
+rest.sigv4-enabled = "true"
+rest.signing-region = "<region>"
+rest.signing-name = "glue"
+```
+
+### Direct Glue Data Catalog
+
+Uses the Glue Data Catalog with a regular S3 bucket for table data. Grant IAM access to both the S3 bucket and the Glue catalog.
+
+```toml
+[destination.iceberg]
+catalog_type = "rest"
+
+[destination.iceberg.credentials]
+uri = "https://glue.<region>.amazonaws.com/iceberg"
+warehouse = "<account-id>"
+
+[destination.iceberg.credentials.properties]
+rest.sigv4-enabled = "true"
+rest.signing-region = "<region>"
+rest.signing-name = "glue"

+---
+
+Run Doc Detective in continuous integration (CI) pipelines using the GitHub Action. Test your docs on every push or pull request.
+
+## Set up the GitHub Action
+
+To add Doc Detective to your GitHub Actions workflow, create a YAML file in your `.github/workflows` directory:
+
+```yaml
+name: doc-detective
+on: [pull_request]
+
+jobs:
+  runTests:
+    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
+    steps:
+      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
+      - uses: doc-detective/github-action@v1
+```
+
+This runs Doc Detective tests whenever a pull request is opened or updated.
+
+## Configuration options
+
+Customize the action with inputs by adding a `with` key to the `uses` block:
+
+```yaml
+- uses: doc-detective/github-action@v1
+  with:
+    version: latest
+    input: ./docs
+    config: .doc-detective.json
+```
+
+### Common inputs
+
+| Input | Default | Description |
+|-------|---------|-------------|
+| `version` | `latest` | Doc Detective version (npm version or tag) |
+| `working_directory` | Repository root | Directory to run the action in |
+| `config` | None | Path to configuration file |
+| `input` | None | Path to input file or directory (overrides config) |
+| `command` | `runTests` | Command to run (`runTests` or `runCoverage`) |
+| `exit_on_fail` | `false` | Exit with non-zero code if tests fail |
+
+## Create pull requests automatically
+
+Doc Detective might update files in your repository when it runs—like refreshing screenshots or updating command output. You can automatically create a pull request with these changes.
+
+```yaml
+name: doc-detective
+on:
+  schedule:
+    - cron: '0 0 * * *'  # Run daily at midnight
+
+jobs:
+  runTests:
+    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
+    permissions:
+      contents: write
+      pull-requests: write
+
+    steps:
+      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
+      - uses: doc-detective/github-action@v1
+        with:
+          create_pr_on_change: true
+          pr_title: Doc Detective found changes
+          pr_labels: doc-detective,for-review
+```
+
+<Note>
+
+You must enable GitHub Actions to create pull requests for your repository. Go to **Settings** > **Actions** > **General** and select **Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests**.
+
+</Note>
+
+### Pull request options
+
+| Input | Default | Description |
+|-------|---------|-------------|
+| `create_pr_on_change` | `false` | Create a PR if files change |
+| `pr_branch` | `doc-detective-{DATE}` | Branch name for the PR |
+| `pr_title` | `Doc Detective Changes` | PR title |
+| `pr_body` | See default | PR description (`$RUN_URL` inserts the workflow URL) |
+| `pr_labels` | `doc-detective` | Comma-separated labels |
+| `pr_assignees` | None | Comma-separated usernames to assign |
+| `pr_reviewers` | None | Comma-separated usernames to request reviews |
+
+## Create issues on test failure
+
+If tests fail, you can automatically create a GitHub issue to track the problem. You can also trigger [integrations](/docs/get-started/integrations) to investigate and fix failures. When you set `integrations`, the action mentions the configured AI integrations in the issue so they can analyze the failures and suggest potential fixes. For details, see [Integrations](/docs/get-started/integrations#get-ai-analysis-of-potential-fixes).
+
+```yaml
+name: doc-detective
+on: [pull_request]
+
+jobs:
+  runTests:
+    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
+    permissions:
+      contents: read
+      issues: write
+    steps:
+      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
+      - uses: doc-detective/github-action@v1
+        with:
+          create_issue_on_fail: true
+          issue_title: Doc Detective found documentation issues
+          integrations: claude
+```
+
+### Issue options
+
+| Input | Default | Description |
+|-------|---------|-------------|
+| `create_issue_on_fail` | `false` | Create an issue if tests fail |
+| `issue_title` | `Doc Detective Failure` | Issue title |
+| `issue_body` | See default | Issue body (`$RESULTS` inserts test results, `$RUN_URL` inserts workflow URL, `$PROMPT` inserts the prompt text) |
+| `issue_labels` | `doc-detective` | Comma-separated labels |
+| `issue_assignees` | None | Comma-separated usernames to assign |
+| `integrations` | None | Comma-separated integrations to trigger (see [Integrations](/docs/get-started/integrations)) |
+| `prompt` | See default | Custom prompt to pass to integrations |
+
+## Action outputs
+
+The action provides outputs you can use in subsequent workflow steps:
+
+| Output | Description |
+|--------|-------------|
+| `results` | JSON-formatted test results |
+| `pull_request_url` | URL of created PR (if applicable) |
+| `issue_url` | URL of created issue (if applicable) |
+
+Example using outputs:
+
+```yaml
+- uses: doc-detective/github-action@v1
+  id: doc-detective
+- run: echo "Results: ${{ steps.doc-detective.outputs.results }}"
+```
+
+## Browser modes
+
+On Ubuntu runners, the action only supports headless browser mode. Chrome and Firefox contexts automatically fall back to headless mode when necessary.
+
+If your tests require non-headless mode (like video recording with `record`), use macOS or Windows runners instead:
+
+```yaml
+jobs:
+  runTests:
+    runs-on: macos-latest  # or windows-latest
+    steps:
+      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
+      - uses: doc-detective/github-action@v1
+```

+
+The [GitHub Action](/docs/get-started/ci) runs your Doc Detective tests on every push or pull request. When a test fails, the action can surface the failure in your repository so that you and your AI integrations can act on it.

+After the issue is created, each configured integration analyzes the failure and responds with an explanation of likely causes and suggested fixes. The analysis appears as a comment on the issue, so you can review the suggestions, apply fixes, and re-run the workflow.

+### 2.3 Narrowing with `as`
+The `as` operator narrows a choice or data-typed expression to a more specific type.
+
+**Syntax**
+`<expression> as <TypeName>`
+
+When applied to a **choice** type, `as` navigates the chain of option attributes to reach the named option, mirroring the path traversal performed by a `switch` case. When applied to a **data** type, it casts to a named subtype.

+**Example:** Narrow a `Vehicle` choice to its `PetrolCar` option and access an attribute of that option.
+```haskell

+```
+
+The `as` operator has the same precedence as the path (`->`) operator and is left-associative, so `foo -> bar as Qux -> attr` parses as `((foo -> bar) as Qux) -> attr`.
+
+The target of `as` must be either a direct option of the choice type or a recognized subtype of the data type, and the expression being narrowed must be of a compatible choice or data type. Otherwise the expression is flagged as invalid.

+---
+title: "Accelerator Setup Guide"
+tags: getting-started
+---
+
+# Contents
+- [Contents](#contents)
+- [Introduction](#introduction)
+- [CPU](#cpu)
+- [Intel XPU](#intel-xpu)
+- [Adding support for other accelerators](#adding-support-for-other-accelerators)
+
+# Introduction
+DeepSpeed can run on a variety of Deep Learning accelerators through the [DeepSpeed Accelerator Abstraction Interface](/tutorials/accelerator-abstraction-interface/). This guide collects the environment setup steps needed to run DeepSpeed on each supported accelerator type. Each accelerator has its own section below; new accelerator types can be added as additional sections following the same structure.
+
+In general, the recommended order is to install the accelerator-specific dependencies (for example, the accelerator extension and its communication library) **before** installing DeepSpeed, since DeepSpeed installation is accelerator related.
+
+# CPU
+DeepSpeed supports using the CPU as an accelerator. A DeepSpeed model written against the DeepSpeed Accelerator Abstraction Interface can run on CPU without changes to the model code. DeepSpeed decides whether _Intel Extension for PyTorch_ is installed in the environment; if this package is installed, DeepSpeed will use CPU as the accelerator, otherwise CUDA device will be used as the accelerator.
+
+To run a DeepSpeed model on CPU, use the following steps to prepare the environment:
+
+```
+python -m pip install intel_extension_for_pytorch
+python -m pip install oneccl_bind_pt -f https://developer.intel.com/ipex-whl-stable-cpu
+git clone https://github.com/oneapi-src/oneCCL
+cd oneCCL
+mkdir build
+cd build
+cmake ..
+make
+make install
+```
+
+Before running a CPU workload, source the oneCCL environment variables:
+
+```
+source <path-to-oneCCL>/build/_install/env/setvars.sh
+```
+
+After the environment is prepared, launch DeepSpeed inference with the following command:
+
+```
+deepspeed --bind_cores_to_rank <deepspeed-model-script>
+```
+
+This command launches a number of workers equal to the number of CPU sockets on the system. Currently DeepSpeed supports running inference models with AutoTP on top of CPU. The argument `--bind_cores_to_rank` distributes CPU cores on the system evenly among workers, allowing each worker to run on a dedicated set of CPU cores.
+
+On a CPU system there might be daemon processes that periodically activate and increase the variance of each worker. One practice is to leave a couple of cores for daemon processes using the `--bind_core_list` argument:
+
+```
+deepspeed --bind_cores_to_rank --bind_core_list 0-51,56-107 <deepspeed-model-script>
+```
+
+The command above leaves 4 cores on each socket to daemon processes (assuming two sockets, each with 56 cores).
+
+You can also set an arbitrary number of workers. Unlike GPU, CPU cores on a host can be further divided into subgroups. When this number is not set, DeepSpeed detects the number of NUMA nodes on the system and launches one worker for each NUMA node:
+
+```
+deepspeed --num_accelerators 4 --bind_cores_to_rank <deepspeed-model-script>
+```
+
+Launching a DeepSpeed model on multiple CPU nodes is similar to other accelerators. Specify `impi` as the launcher and `--bind_cores_to_rank` for better core binding. Also specify the `slots` number according to the number of CPU sockets in the host file:
+
+```
+# hostfile content should follow the format
+# worker-1-hostname slots=<#sockets>
+# worker-2-hostname slots=<#sockets>
+# ...
+
+deepspeed --hostfile=<hostfile> --bind_cores_to_rank --launcher impi --master_addr <master-ip> <deepspeed-model-script>
+```
+
+# Intel XPU
+DeepSpeed supports running on Intel XPU (Intel data center GPUs) through the _Intel Extension for DeepSpeed_. DeepSpeed checks whether the extension is installed in the environment to decide whether to use the accelerator backend provided by that extension.
+
+To run a DeepSpeed model on Intel XPU:
+
+1. Install _Intel Extension for DeepSpeed_ following the instructions in the [intel-extension-for-deepspeed repository](https://github.com/intel/intel-extension-for-deepspeed/).
+2. Install DeepSpeed in the same environment.
+3. Run your model as usual; DeepSpeed will detect the installed extension and use the XPU accelerator backend.
+
+`CUDA_Accelerator` is the default accelerator in DeepSpeed. If no other DeepSpeed accelerator extension is installed, `CUDA_Accelerator` will be used.
+
+When running a model on different accelerators in a cloud environment, the recommended practice is to provision an environment for each accelerator in a different env with tools such as _anaconda/miniconda/virtualenv_, and load the appropriate env when running models on each accelerator.
+
+Note that different accelerators may have different 'flavor' of float16 or bfloat16. It is recommended to make the model configurable for both float16 and bfloat16, so that model code does not need to be changed when running on different accelerators.
+
+# Adding support for other accelerators
+Support for a new accelerator type can be added by implementing a DeepSpeed accelerator extension. An accelerator extension contains:
+1. An `XYZ_Accelerator(DeepSpeedAccelerator)` class definition, where 'XYZ' is the accelerator name, such as 'XPU' or 'CPU'. This class implements `class DeepSpeedAccelerator` and will be returned by `get_accelerator()` in DeepSpeed.
+2. Op builders following the [intel-extension-for-deepspeed op_builder directory](https://github.com/intel/intel-extension-for-deepspeed/tree/main/intel_extension_for_deepspeed/op_builder). All op builders need to inherit `deepspeed.ops.op_builder.builder.OpBuilder` directly or indirectly. A common practice is to implement a base op builder (SYCLOpBuilder in the case of Intel Extension for DeepSpeed) and inherit this base op builder instead.
+3. Op kernels as in the [intel-extension-for-deepspeed csrc directory](https://github.com/intel/intel-extension-for-deepspeed/tree/main/intel_extension_for_deepspeed/op_builder/csrc).
+
+An extension does not have to implement all op builders under [DeepSpeed op_builder](https://github.com/microsoft/DeepSpeed/tree/master/op_builder) at once. A missing op builder usually means a certain DeepSpeed functionality cannot be used for that accelerator, but models that do not use that functionality can still run.
+
+When the accelerator extension is installed in the environment, it can be used by either explicitly calling `deepspeed.accelerator.set_accelerator(XYZ_Accelerator())` following the example in [real_accelerator.py](https://github.com/microsoft/DeepSpeed/blob/master/accelerator/real_accelerator.py), or by adding implicit detection code in `get_accelerator` in the same file.
+
+For more details on writing accelerator-agnostic models and implementing accelerator extensions, see the [DeepSpeed Accelerator Abstraction Interface](/tutorials/accelerator-abstraction-interface/) tutorial.

+Coalescing Gradient Reduction Across Multiple Backward Calls
+~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
+.. autofunction:: deepspeed.DeepSpeedEngine.coalesce_grad_reduction
+
+When you issue multiple ``engine.backward()`` calls within a single optimizer
+step (for example, cached contrastive losses or custom autograd functions),
+ZeRO stages 1, 2, and 3 normally reduce gradients on every backward. Wrap the
+backwards in ``engine.coalesce_grad_reduction()`` to defer the reduction and
+issue a single reduction pass on context exit, before the next ``engine.step()``:
+
+.. code-block:: python
+
+    for batch in data_loader:
+        with model_engine.coalesce_grad_reduction():
+            for chunk in cached_chunks:
+                loss = model_engine(chunk)
+                model_engine.backward(loss)
+        model_engine.step()
+
+One ``with`` block corresponds to one optimizer step. The following are not
+supported and raise an error:
+
+* Calling ``engine.step()`` inside the block.
+* Nesting with ``engine.no_sync()``.
+* ZeRO stage 0, pipeline parallelism, and the BF16/FP16 optimizer wrappers
+  (``NotImplementedError``).
+

+## Historical cluster workload costs
+
+The queries above estimate costs from the current allocation and pricing metrics. To calculate historical costs that match the numbers shown in the OpenCost UI (and to graph them in tools such as Grafana), query the allocation metrics that OpenCost records over time. These metrics are emitted with the `container_cpu_allocation`, `container_memory_allocation_bytes`, and related series, and are aggregated per workload using the `namespace`, `pod`, and `container` labels.
+
+__Hourly cost of a workload over a time range__
+
+Use a range query (for example in Grafana, set the query type to `Range`) and adjust the `namespace` and `pod` matchers to the workload you want to inspect:
+
+```
+sum(
+  (
+    container_cpu_allocation{namespace="default"}
+      * on(instance) group_left() node_cpu_hourly_cost
+    + container_memory_allocation_bytes{namespace="default"} / 1024 / 1024 / 1024
+      * on(instance) group_left() node_ram_hourly_cost
+  )
+) by (namespace, pod)
+```
+
+__Total cost of a workload over a time range__
+
+To get the total cost for a window rather than an hourly rate, wrap the hourly query in `sum_over_time` and multiply by the scrape interval in hours. For a 1 minute scrape interval this is `1/60`:
+
+```
+sum_over_time(
+  (
+    sum(
+      container_cpu_allocation{namespace="default"}
+        * on(instance) group_left() node_cpu_hourly_cost
+      + container_memory_allocation_bytes{namespace="default"} / 1024 / 1024 / 1024
+        * on(instance) group_left() node_ram_hourly_cost
+    ) by (namespace, pod)
+  )[1h:1m]
+) * (1 / 60)
+```
+
+__Daily cost of a workload over the last 30 days__
+
+```

+    (
+      container_cpu_allocation{namespace="default"}
+        * on(instance) group_left() node_cpu_hourly_cost
+      + container_memory_allocation_bytes{namespace="default"} / 1024 / 1024 / 1024

-You can configure authentication in your OpenFGA server in two ways: no authentication (the default) or pre-shared key authentication.
+You can configure authentication in your OpenFGA server in three ways: no authentication (the default), pre-shared key authentication, or OIDC authentication.
 
-If using **Pre-shared key authentication**, you will configure OpenFGA with a secret key and your application calling OpenFGA will have to set an `Authorization: Bearer <YOUR-KEY-HERE>` header. You can configure multiple keys.
+#### Pre-shared Key Authentication
+
+With **pre-shared key authentication**, you configure OpenFGA with one or more secret keys, and every client calling OpenFGA must send one of those keys in an `Authorization: Bearer <YOUR-KEY-HERE>` header. Requests that omit the header or send an unknown key are rejected with an HTTP `401 Unauthorized` response.
+
+You can configure the keys in your `config.yaml`:
+
+```yaml
+authn:
+  method: preshared
+  preshared:
+    keys: ["key1", "key2"]
+```
+
+Or with environment variables (which take priority over the configuration file):
+
+```shell
+docker run -p 8080:8080 -p 8081:8081 openfga/openfga run \
+    --authn-method preshared \
+    --authn-preshared-keys "key1,key2"
+```
+
+```shell
+# Equivalent using environment variables
+docker run -p 8080:8080 -p 8081:8081 \
+    -e OPENFGA_AUTHN_METHOD=preshared \
+    -e OPENFGA_AUTHN_PRESHARED_KEYS="key1,key2" \
+    openfga/openfga run
+```
+
+:::caution Warning
+If you configure pre-shared keys but still receive `401 Unauthorized` responses, verify that:
+- the `authn.method` is set to `preshared` (setting only the keys is not enough),
+- the client sends the key as `Authorization: Bearer <key>` (not as a query parameter or custom header),
+- the key sent by the client exactly matches one of the configured keys, and
+- environment variables are prefixed with `OPENFGA_` and use the correct name (e.g. `OPENFGA_AUTHN_PRESHARED_KEYS`).
+:::
+
+#### OIDC Authentication
+
+With **OIDC authentication**, OpenFGA validates the bearer token sent by the client against an OIDC issuer. Clients obtain a token from the issuer and send it as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`.
+
+```yaml
+authn:
+  method: oidc
+  oidc:
+    issuer: https://issuer.example.com
+    audience: https://api.example.com
+```
+
+Or with environment variables:
+
+```shell
+docker run -p 8080:8080 -p 8081:8081 \
+    -e OPENFGA_AUTHN_METHOD=oidc \
+    -e OPENFGA_AUTHN_OIDC_ISSUER=https://issuer.example.com \
+    -e OPENFGA_AUTHN_OIDC_AUDIENCE=https://api.example.com \
+    openfga/openfga run
+```
+
+:::caution Warning
+If you are going to use either authentication method in production, you should enable TLS in your OpenFGA server.
+:::
+
+#### Configuring TLS
+
+TLS is configured with the `--http-tls-cert`, `--http-tls-key`, `--grpc-tls-cert`, and `--grpc-tls-key` flags (or the corresponding `OPENFGA_HTTP_TLS_CERT`, `OPENFGA_HTTP_TLS_KEY`, `OPENFGA_GRPC_TLS_CERT`, and `OPENFGA_GRPC_TLS_KEY` environment variables).
+
+Paths are resolved relative to the working directory of the OpenFGA process. When running in Docker, the files must exist **inside the container**, so mount them into the container and reference the mounted path:
+
+```shell
+docker run -p 8080:8080 -p 8081:8081 \
+    -v "$PWD/certs:/certs" \
+    -e OPENFGA_HTTP_TLS_ENABLED=true \
+    -e OPENFGA_HTTP_TLS_CERT=/certs/server.crt \
+    -e OPENFGA_HTTP_TLS_KEY=/certs/server.key \
+    openfga/openfga run
+```
 
 :::caution Warning
-If you are going to use this setup in production, you should enable TLS in your OpenFGA server.
+A missing-file error when configuring TLS usually means the path is not visible to the OpenFGA process. Confirm the certificate and key files exist at the configured path inside the container (or on the host when running the binary directly) and that the path is absolute or relative to the process working directory.

+
+When you shard your test runs (for example, across multiple CI jobs), each shard produces its own coverage data. To apply a coverage threshold to the combined result, first collect the per-shard coverage output, then combine it before checking the threshold.

+```

+Finally, apply the threshold to the combined data with `coverage report --fail-under`:
+
+```bash
+❯ python -m coverage report --fail-under=70

+## `CompositeProcess`
+
+Sometimes you need to run multiple commands in a single `Process` invocation, for example to ensure that a setup step and a subsequent step share the same sandbox (which matters in the presence of remote caching or remote execution). `CompositeProcess` composes multiple `Subprocess` instances into a single `Process`, executed sequentially via a Bash script. Execution stops on the first non-zero exit code.
+
+```python
+from pants.engine.composite_process import CompositeProcess, Subprocess
+from pants.engine.process import ProcessResult
+from pants.engine.rules import rule
+
+@rule
+async def demo(...) -> Foo:
+    result: ProcessResult = await execute_process_or_raise(**implicitly(
+        CompositeProcess(
+            [
+                Subprocess(argv=["/bin/echo", "first step"]),
+                Subprocess(command="echo second step"),
+            ],
+            description="Run two steps in one Process.",
+        )
+    ))
+```
+
+Each `Subprocess` accepts either a pre-joined `command: str` or an `argv: Iterable[str]`, but not both. It also accepts the same per-subprocess fields as `Process`: `input_digest`, `immutable_input_digests`, `env`, `append_only_caches`, `output_files`, and `output_directories`.
+
+When the `CompositeProcess` is converted to a `Process`, the input digests of all subprocesses are merged, and the output files, output directories, environment variables, and append-only caches are combined. If two subprocesses set the same environment variable, immutable input digest path, or append-only cache name to different values, an error is raised.
+
+`CompositeProcess` also supports the process-level fields `description`, `level`, `use_nailgun`, `working_directory`, `timeout_seconds`, `jdk_home`, `execution_slot_variable`, `concurrency_available`, `concurrency`, `cache_scope`, `remote_cache_speculation_delay_millis`, and `attempt`. Use `prepend_subprocesses()` and `append_subprocesses()` to add steps, and `CompositeProcess.from_process()` to wrap an existing `Process`.

+### Sharing packages between environments
+
+Because the cache is shared, Pixi does not need to download or unpack the same package twice.
+When a package is installed into an environment, Pixi links it from the cache into the environment's prefix instead of copying it.
+On most platforms this is done with hardlinks, so the package data on disk is stored only once even though it appears in multiple environments.
+
+This means that having several environments that depend on the same packages does not multiply their disk usage.
+For example, if your `default` and `cuda` environments both use `python` and `numpy`, those packages are stored once in the cache and linked into both `.pixi/envs/default` and `.pixi/envs/cuda`.
+Only packages that are unique to an environment add to its disk usage.
+
+A few caveats apply:
+
+- Hardlinks require the cache and the environments to live on the same filesystem. If they are on different filesystems (for example when using [detached environments](../reference/pixi_configuration.md#detached-environments) on another drive), Pixi falls back to copying the files, and the packages will take up space in each environment.

+hierarchical key-value system) whose keys form a tree, mirroring the groups and arrays

+## Handling `UNSET` and `Maybe`
+
+`strawberry.asdict` differs from `dataclasses.asdict` in a few ways to better
+match Strawberry's semantics:
+
+- Fields whose value is `UNSET` are omitted from the returned dictionary
+  entirely.
+- Fields explicitly set to `None` are preserved.
+- `Some(value)` containers are unwrapped, returning their `value` only.
+- For fields annotated with `Maybe`, a value of `None` is converted back to
+  `UNSET` (and therefore omitted).
+
+These rules apply recursively to nested dataclasses, lists, and dictionaries.
+
+```python
+import strawberry
+from strawberry import UNSET, Maybe, Some
+
+
+@strawberry.input
+class Filter:
+    name: Maybe[str] = UNSET
+    age: Maybe[int] = Some(30)
+
+
+# should be {"age": 30}
+filter_dict = strawberry.asdict(Filter())
+```
+
+Because the transformation uses a shallow copy rather than re-instantiating the
+dataclass, `__init__`/`__post_init__` are not called and `init=False` fields are
+supported. Frozen dataclasses are also supported.

+---
+title: Pydantic Error Extension
+summary: Add structured Pydantic validation error details to GraphQL errors.
+tags: pydantic, errors
+---
+
+# `PydanticErrorExtension`
+
+This extension enriches GraphQL errors caused by a Pydantic `ValidationError`
+with structured details. After an operation executes, any error whose original
+error is a Pydantic `ValidationError` gets its `extensions` field populated with
+a `validation_errors` list. Each entry contains:
+
+- `field`: the dot-joined location path of the failing field
+- `message`: the validation message from Pydantic
+
+<Note>
+
+The extension is a no-op when Pydantic is not installed.
+
+</Note>
+
+## Usage example:
+
+```python
+import strawberry
+from strawberry.extensions import PydanticErrorExtension
+
+schema = strawberry.Schema(
+    query=Query,
+    mutation=Mutation,
+    extensions=[PydanticErrorExtension],
+)
+```
+
+When a mutation raises a Pydantic `ValidationError`, the resulting GraphQL error
+will include the structured details, for example:
+
+```json
+{
+  "errors": [
+    {
+      "message": "...",
+      "extensions": {
+        "validation_errors": [
+          { "field": "age", "message": "Input should be greater than 18" }
+        ]
+      }
+    }
+  ]
+}
+```

+# Strict Content-Type { #strict-content-type }
+
+By default, **FastAPI** is strict about the `Content-Type` header of incoming requests that carry a body.
+
+If a request includes a body but does not include a `Content-Type` header, **FastAPI** will **not** parse the body as JSON, and the request will be rejected with a `422 Unprocessable Entity` response.
+
+## Why Strict Content-Type? { #why-strict-content-type }
+
+This prevents potential cross-site request forgery (CSRF) attacks that exploit the browser's ability to send requests without a `Content-Type` header, bypassing CORS preflight checks. This is particularly relevant for apps that need to be run locally (in localhost).
+
+## Disable Strict Content-Type { #disable-strict-content-type }
+
+You can disable this behavior by setting the `strict_content_type` parameter to `False` on the `FastAPI` application:
+
+```python
+from fastapi import FastAPI
+
+app = FastAPI(strict_content_type=False)
+```
+
+With this setting, requests without a `Content-Type` header will have their body parsed as JSON, which maintains compatibility with certain clients that don't send `Content-Type` headers.
+
+You can also set it on an `APIRouter`:
+
+```python
+from fastapi import APIRouter
+
+router = APIRouter(strict_content_type=False)
+```
+
+## Inheritance { #inheritance }
+
+The setting participates in the existing inheritance chain: a value explicitly set on a router overrides whatever the parent application specifies, while routers that leave the parameter at its default pick up the parent's value. Nested router configurations follow the same resolution order.
+
+## Explicit Content-Type { #explicit-content-type }
+
+Requests that include an explicit `Content-Type: application/json` header are unaffected by this setting and continue to be parsed as JSON as before.
